why: An FDE's work is invisible until it is demonstrated: the system you spent six weeks deploying inside a customer's VPC gets renewed, expanded or killed on the strength of ten minutes in front of people who will never read your code. The room is not friendly by default - the CFO is looking for the line item to cut, the platform lead is calculating whose pager this lands on, and both will test whether you can defend a trade-off you actually made rather than recite a script. This is the one skill where being right is worth nothing unless you can show it live, price it, and hold the number under attack.
prerequisites: Discovery (topic 66): you must already know the customer's real workflow, their current cycle time, and who owns the budget - a demo without a discovered baseline has nothing to compare against.

Engagement documents (topic 67): ADRs, SOW and design-doc discipline, because every number you say out loud in a demo has a habit of turning up in a contract, and every trade-off you defend should already exist as a written decision record.

SRE fundamentals (topic 20): SLI vs SLO vs SLA, error budgets, measurement windows and exclusions - so you can tell the difference between a demo observation and something you are allowed to commit to.

Cloud cost and FinOps (topic 19) plus cost and latency engineering (topic 59): unit economics, marginal vs fixed cost, prompt caching and batching, so the cost question is answered with a sheet rather than a shrug.

A real system of your own to show - the Hermes Agent deployment (topic 52) or the Dokeo assistant - deployed somewhere reproducible, with LLM observability (topic 54) already wired so you can display traces, token cost and p95 during the demo.
Enough delivery fluency with Docker Compose, seeded Postgres fixtures and pinned image digests (topics 5, 6, 29) that a clean-clone cold start is a routine operation, not a rehearsal risk.

subtopics.name: Read the room: five roles, five different kill switches
subtopics.learn: Before writing a single slide, name the actual humans and what each one can veto: the economic buyer (payback period, headcount, is this a new line item), the technical champion (needs to look correct for having backed you), the blocker (platform lead or CISO whose on-call rotation absorbs this), the end user (whose job changes shape), and the finance analyst who will re-derive your arithmetic afterwards. For each role write the single question they will ask and the single artifact that answers it in under 60 seconds. Then rehearse the same ten minutes twice, re-ordered for two different rooms, so you learn that the demo is a playlist, not a script.

resource.label: Atlassian Team Playbook - DACI: decision roles and who actually approves

subtopics.name: The ten-minute spine: claim, pain, live proof, cost, ask
subtopics.learn: Fix a segment budget and hold it: 60s one-sentence claim, 90s their current workflow stated in their own numbers, 5 minutes of the thing actually running on their data shape, 90s cost and operational reality, 60s a specific ask. Enforce two rules that most engineers break - no architecture diagram before minute seven, and never demo a capability you cannot attach to a named workflow the customer described in discovery. Practise with a visible timer; when a segment runs over by more than 20% you cut content, you never talk faster.

resource.label: Sequoia Capital - Writing a Business Plan (purpose, problem, solution, model, ask)

subtopics.name: The first sixty seconds and the one-sentence claim
subtopics.learn: Write one declarative sentence containing a measured number in the unit the buyer already tracks: 'your claims team spends 11 minutes per case today; this does it in 40 seconds on last week's real queue.' Then cut it to under 25 words, active voice, no hedging verbs, no product name in the first clause. Ban every form of throat-clearing - no 'so basically', no team introduction, no tool tour, no apology for the environment - and rehearse the line until you can deliver it while your laptop is still waking the display.

resource.label: Google Technical Writing One - Short sentences (one idea per sentence, cut needless words)

subtopics.name: Demo environment as a shipped artifact
subtopics.learn: Treat the demo like production: a clean clone must reach a working system with one command in under three minutes, images pinned by digest rather than a floating :latest tag, and seed data restored from a checked-in dump or SQL fixture containing realistic but wholly synthetic names. Tag the exact state in git (demo-2026-03-12) so you can reproduce the run six weeks later when someone asks what they saw, and pre-pull every image the night before. Rehearse a cold boot on the machine, display resolution and network you will actually use - corporate guest wifi, the HDMI or Zoom share path, terminal at 16pt or larger, browser zoom at 125-150% - because half of all demo failures are environmental, not technical.

resource.label: Docker Compose Quickstart - one-command multi-service stack with volumes and healthchecks

subtopics.name: Determinism: making an LLM demo reproducible
subtopics.learn: Set temperature 0 with top_p 1, pin an exact model id rather than a floating alias, freeze the prompt version by hash, and put a request cache keyed on (model_id, prompt_hash, input_hash) in front of every call - and understand that temperature 0 is still not bit-identical across providers or batch conditions, so the cache is your only real guarantee. Build a replay mode (DEMO_REPLAY=1) that serves cached responses with a realistic simulated delay, so a provider incident or a 40-second tail latency degrades into a smooth demo instead of dead air. Set explicit client timeouts and max_tokens so a hang surfaces as a fast fallback, and fire one throwaway warm-up request before you present.

resource.label: Claude Developer Platform Docs (models, parameters, prompt caching)

subtopics.name: Capture rig and the tape-review loop
subtopics.learn: Record at 1080p30, capture a single window rather than the whole desktop, run a clean browser profile with no bookmarks or other customers' tabs, and put the OS into do-not-disturb before the first take. Get audio right once - a cheap cardioid at speaking distance, peaks around -12 to -6 dBFS - because bad audio makes a competent engineer sound uncertain. Then review the tape with a stopwatch and log four hard numbers per take: time-to-first-visible-value, seconds of dead air, filler words per minute, and the number of times you said 'I'll come back to that'. Do a second pass at 2x with the sound off to test whether the screen alone tells the story.

resource.label: OBS Studio Quick Start Guide - sources, window capture and audio mixer setup

subtopics.name: Failure drills: the demo breaks at minute four
subtopics.learn: Adopt a hard rule - 30 seconds of live debugging, then switch - and build the switch beforehand: a three-minute pre-recorded clip of the identical flow on the identical data sitting on local disk, a phone hotspot already paired, and a second machine booted with the demo warm. Rehearse the exact sentence you say when it breaks: name what failed, say what you are doing, keep moving, and do not apologise twice. Deliberately sabotage a rehearsal - kill the database container or drop the network at minute four - and time your recovery, because a clean recovery is itself the most persuasive reliability evidence in the room.

resource.label: Principles of Chaos Engineering - deliberate failure injection to build confidence

subtopics.name: Show the instrumentation, not the slide
subtopics.learn: During the demo, pull up one board or one trace covering the run the room just watched: p95 latency, cost per request, token counts, error rate, and the retrieval or tool calls that produced the answer. This converts 'it works on your laptop' into 'it is measured', and it pre-empts the cost question by putting the number on screen before anyone asks. Keep it to a single board with at most four panels and a time range that actually contains the demo - a wall of graphs reads as noise, and an empty panel reads as a lie.

subtopics.name: Translating engineering into money, risk and time
subtopics.learn: Do the arithmetic out loud as a visible chain - cases per month x minutes saved x loaded hourly cost = dollars per year - and always separate the assumption row from the result row so the CFO argues with the assumption instead of with you. Learn the three currencies executives actually trade in: dollars (opex, avoided headcount), risk (audit findings, breach exposure, SLA credits, regulatory deadline), and time (weeks to launch, sooner revenue). Then state explicitly what you are not claiming; volunteering the boundary of your claim is what makes the rest of it credible.

resource.label: FinOps Framework - Quantify Business Value domain (mapping tech cost to business outcomes)

subtopics.name: The unit-economics sheet a CFO cannot dent
subtopics.learn: Build one page, denominated per 1,000 requests: input and output tokens at list price, retrieval and database, compute, egress, human review minutes, and amortised build cost. Add a sensitivity block - 10x volume, 50% model price cut, cache hit rates of 0/40/80%, batch versus interactive - plus payback period and break-even volume, and know the marginal-versus-fixed split cold because 'what happens when we go from 10,000 to 1,000,000 calls a month' needs a number and a slope, not an adjective. Keep the provider's own pricing page open in a background tab so any challenged figure is one click from its source.

resource.label: Amazon Bedrock Pricing - per-token list price, batch vs on-demand tiers

subtopics.name: Defending a trade-off: options table, rejected alternatives, one-way doors
subtopics.learn: For every decision likely to be attacked, arrive with a three-row options table scored on cost, latency, operational burden, time-to-first-value and blast radius, plus the specific reason each rejected option was rejected and the evidence that would change your mind. Separate reversible two-way doors (model choice, chunking strategy, dashboard layout - decide fast, say so) from one-way doors (tenancy boundary, data model, where customer data physically lands) and defend them at different intensities. Write it as an ADR before the demo with context, decision, consequences and alternatives, so under pressure you are retrieving a considered position rather than inventing one.

subtopics.name: Committing to numbers: p95, availability, and what you will actually sign
subtopics.learn: Know your own p50/p95/p99 under realistic concurrency rather than from a single warm request, and say out loud which figures are demo observations and which you would sign as an SLO. Never commit an availability number without also stating the measurement window, the error budget it implies, and the exclusions (their IdP, their VPN, their upstream ERP), because 99.9% over 30 days and 99.9% over 12 months are different products. Practise the refusal: 'I will not commit to that in this room; I will send you a measured number with the methodology by Thursday' - since anything you say casually here is liable to be pasted verbatim into the SOW.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives

subtopics.name: Hostile question taxonomy and the answer-first pattern
subtopics.learn: Classify the question in the first three seconds - factual gap, scope probe, budget attack, credibility attack, 'we tried this before', or a trap built on a false premise - because each has a different response shape. Answer first in one sentence, give one sentence of reason, then stop talking; correct a false premise explicitly before answering it; and when you do not know, say so with a named method and a date rather than improvising. Never renegotiate scope live. Rehearse the fourth follow-up specifically, since hostility works by repetition and it is consistency across three restatements that earns trust; when the attack is about a past failure, describe it factually and blamelessly the way a good postmortem does.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure

subtopics.name: The standing objection set: build-vs-buy, lock-in, data handling, model risk
subtopics.learn: Pre-write and rehearse a 60-second answer for the four objections that appear in every enterprise room. Build-vs-buy: answer in engineering-months plus ongoing maintenance and eval upkeep, not feature parity. Lock-in: name precisely what is portable (prompts, eval sets, retrieval corpus, your own data) versus what is not. Data handling: where data flows, retention, training opt-out, residency, subprocessors, and who can read it - have the one-page data-flow diagram ready as a leave-behind. Model risk: your measured error rate on their eval set, where the human approves, and what the audit trail records.

resource.label: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) - model risk, data handling, governance

subtopics.name: Q&A choreography and the close
subtopics.learn: Compress and restate each question before answering so the room hears the version you are answering, and park anything needing more than two minutes into a named follow-up with an owner and a date rather than derailing the session. Reserve the final 60 seconds for a concrete ask on screen - a pilot scope, a named dataset, a specific access request, a decision date - because ending on 'any questions?' hands the close to whoever in the room is least invested. Send the follow-up within 24 hours containing exactly the artifacts you promised and nothing extra.

resource.label: MIT OpenCourseWare - Patrick Winston, How to Speak (handling questions, how to stop)

subtopics.name: The four-take ladder and a scoring rubric that bites
subtopics.learn: Score every recorded take 0-2 on ten dimensions: claim clarity, time-to-first-visible-value, live-versus-slides ratio, telemetry shown, unit economics defended, trade-off defended with named alternatives, answer-first rate on hostile questions, seconds of dead air, filler words per minute, and specificity of the close. Structure the ladder deliberately - take 1 cold with notes, take 2 with no notes, take 3 with a recruited hostile questioner briefed to interrupt on cost and scope, take 4 with a failure injected at minute four. Diff the scores across takes and only re-record once you can name the exact line or segment you are changing, otherwise you are just accumulating footage.

resource.label: Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center - Creating and Using Rubrics (criteria, descriptors, performance levels)

subtopics.name: No-slides fallback: three boxes and an arrow
subtopics.learn: Be able to draw the entire system in three boxes and an arrow in 90 seconds on a whiteboard or tablet - the trust boundary and ingress, the thing that does the work, and where state lives - naming where their data resides, where the model call happens, and where a human approves. Keep three zoom levels ready: three boxes for the CFO, eight for the platform lead, and the real deployment diagram for the architect, and switch level based on the question rather than showing the biggest one you have. Rehearse this standing up with a marker, because it is what you do when the room has no screen or the projector dies.

resource.label: Azure Architecture Center (reference architectures and diagrams)

outcomes: You can deliver a ten-minute demo with no notes and hit measured targets on the tape: first visible value under 90 seconds, under 15 seconds of total dead air, and fewer than three filler words per minute.

You can stand the whole demo up from a clean clone on a machine you have never used in under five minutes, with digest-pinned images and seeded synthetic data, and reproduce the identical run six weeks later from a git tag.

You can answer 'what does this cost us at a million requests a month' with a number, the marginal-versus-fixed split, and a sensitivity row, straight off a one-page unit-economics sheet you built yourself.

You can defend any architectural choice in the demo with three considered options, the specific rejection reason for each, and the evidence that would change your mind - sourced from an ADR written before the meeting.
You can lose the network or the model provider at minute four and be back on a pre-recorded fallback within 30 seconds, narrating the failure once and continuing without apology.
You can distinguish out loud between a demo observation and a committable SLO, and decline to commit any availability or latency number without stating its measurement window and exclusions.
You can score your own four recordings against a ten-dimension rubric and show monotonic improvement, naming for each take the specific change that produced the delta.
You can answer the four standing objections - build-vs-buy, lock-in, data handling, model risk - in under 60 seconds each, with a leave-behind artifact for each.
failureModes: The demo runs against :latest images and a live provider endpoint, and a model deprecation or an unnoticed prompt-template change three days before the QBR turns a rehearsed flow into a wrong answer in front of the buyer.

The 'synthetic' seed data was quietly derived from a previous customer's export, a real company name appears on screen, and the meeting stops being a deal conversation and becomes a security incident.

Full-desktop screen sharing leaks a Slack notification, a calendar invite naming another prospect, or a terminal with a live credential in scrollback, and the customer's security lead notices before you do.
The CFO asks what it costs and the answer is 'it's pretty cheap', which converts a signable pilot into a three-week finance review and strands the champion with no numbers to defend internally.

A number said casually in the room - 'sub-200ms p95, 99.9% availability' - is copied verbatim into the SOW by the account team, and six weeks later it is a contractual obligation nobody sized or instrumented.
Everything is shown on a hand-picked happy path, the champion tries one genuinely messy record the next morning, it fails, and the internal narrative becomes 'it only works in their demo'.

Live debugging runs six minutes past the failure because the presenter cannot let go, consuming the entire defence segment so the trade-off and cost questions are never answered and the meeting ends unresolved.
interviewQuestions: You have ten minutes with a CFO who has already decided this project is over budget, and you are the engineer who built it. What is on screen in minute one, what do you deliberately not show at all, and what is your ask at minute ten?

Walk me through a technical decision you had to defend to someone who could cancel the project. What was the actual trade-off, what did they push hardest on, and what did you change afterwards as a result?

Your live demo hangs at minute four - the model call has not returned in 20 seconds and the room is silent. Tell me exactly what you do in the next 30 seconds, and what you had to prepare in advance for that answer to be possible.
A customer's VP asks in the demo whether you can hold 100ms p95 and 99.99% availability. You genuinely do not know. What do you say in the room, and what actually happens downstream if you say yes?

Design the demo environment for a system you will show to twenty different prospects over a quarter. What is pinned, what is seeded, what is faked or replayed, how do you keep it honest, and what breaks first as the product changes underneath it?

Compute cost per 1,000 requests for an LLM feature in front of me. Now the customer tells you their real volume is 20x your assumption and their documents are three times longer - which parts of your number move, and which do not?
The champion loved the demo, and two weeks later the platform team blocks the rollout. What did you fail to do during that demo, and what is your recovery plan for the next meeting?
proofOfWork: Ship a public 'demo kit' repository that makes the four recorded demos reproducible and defensible by someone who was not in the room. It contains a one-command cold-start environment (Compose file with digest-pinned images, a checked-in synthetic seed dump, a documented DEMO_REPLAY mode that serves cached model responses with realistic simulated latency) tagged per demo date so any recording can be re-run byte-for-byte; a defence pack holding the one-page unit-economics sheet with its sensitivity block, three ADRs covering the decisions most likely to be attacked, a one-page data-flow and retention diagram, and an objection matrix of twenty questions each with a written sub-60-second answer; a failure kit with the pre-recorded fallback clip, an asciinema capture of the terminal path, and a written 30-second recovery script; and a RUBRIC.md plus a scores table showing all four takes graded on the ten dimensions with the delta and the specific change that produced it. The README opens with the one-sentence claim and a 90-second architecture sketch in three boxes, so the repo itself demonstrates the skill it documents.
